00.text: A quick guide to the Occupation Detail page.

01.text: For one occupation, the page shows how every visa stream treats it.

02.text: Is the stream inviting? What score was enough? How often does it invite?

03.text: SkillSelect streams sit at the top. Labour market analytics follow below.

04.text: Three filters: Period, State or Territory, and Visa Subclass.

05.text: One visa at a time. The default is subclass one-ninety.

06.text: The filter bar stays at the top while you scroll.

07.text: The header names the occupation and its J-S-A shortage rating.

08.text: The ring compares invitations with the pool: about one percent here.

09.text: The KPIs follow the filters. Here: subclass one-ninety, all states, the last 12 months.

10.text: Estimated Invitations adds up monthly snapshots, so one invitation can count twice.

11.text: Live Job Ads and 2030 Growth are for all of Australia and ignore the filters.

12.text: Each card is one stream: one state and one visa.

13.text: Latest Cutoff: the lowest invited score at the most recent invitation, with its month.

14.text: Invited in 9 of the last 12 months shows how regularly the state invites.

15.text: Status is Active, Quiet, or No invitations. The info icon explains why.

16.text: The Northern Territory invited at 70 points in August. New South Wales has the largest pool, but has been quiet since April.

17.text: Switch to Table to compare every stream in one view.

18.text: Pick one month and each card shows whether the state invited in that month.

19.text: June 2026: 7 of 8 states invited. New South Wales invited nobody.

20.text: Pick a state, and the KPIs follow: South Australia, one invitation, from a pool of 3,846.

21.text: Subclass one-eighty-nine and four-ninety-one Family are national: one card, and the state filter is disabled.

22.text: Detailed Analytics has four tabs. E-O-I and Invitations comes first.

23.text: These are the same charts as the E-O-I Analysis page, for this occupation only.

24.text: Over a period, Invited adds up every month. The most invited score here is 95 points.

25.text: Demand and Vacancies: is there a labour shortage in Australia?

26.text: J-S-A rates Software Engineer as No Shortage. The D-E-W-R shortage list had it in all 8 states up to 2024.

27.text: Online job ads: 3,049 last month, down one percent, and 95 percent in major cities.

28.text: Workforce and Demographics: who does this job in Australia?

29.text: 195,400 people are employed, and the number is growing. Employers get 61 applicants per vacancy, but only 6 are suitable.

30.text: Most workers are 25 to 44. J-S-A expects 15.7 percent growth by 2030.

31.text: Regional and A-I Forecasts: where the jobs are, and where shortages may come.

32.text: About 9.5 percent of Software Engineers work outside the major cities.

33.text: The A-I forecast is a model estimate of shortage risk per state, up to 2030.

34.text: Cutoffs have a date. Invitations are snapshots. National data ignores the filters.
